episodes.211926: A cluster of severe t-storms developed across north central Kansas during the evening of May 17th.  Storms produced damaging winds and large hail.
episodes.212002: During the afternoon, evening, and late evening hours of May 18th, supercells brought severe weather to far NW Missouri. Storms eventually congealed into a large line of thunderstorms, which brought widespread damaging wind gusts to the region as well as a couple tornadoes.
episodes.212011: During the late afternoon, and into the evening, numerous thunderstorms formed over Northwest Kansas in the vicinity of a sharpening dryline. One of them produced hail up to baseball size over and near Goodland. This same storm also produced wind gusts over 80 mph at the Goodland airport. The storm near Goodland produced a brief tornado southwest of Edson as it merged with another storm. As thunderstorms moved eastward, they continued to produce straight-line winds across Thomas, Sheridan, Graham, Norton, and Gove counties.  Over 40 power poles were snapped in Sheridan County, and a machine shed north of Hoxie sustained damage.  Dust storm conditions were reported on the south edge of the thunderstorm activity as the storms moved east over northern Gove County.
episodes.212012: During the 18th midday and afternoon hours, a fast-moving line of severe thunderstorms swept through central Indiana, producing widespread damaging straight line winds.  The severe weather entered the western portions of the IND CWA shortly after 1200 EST, with initial damage reported in Parke and Clay Counties where multiple trees and three power poles were downed.  The line tracked quickly eastward through the early afternoon, impacting the Indianapolis metropolitan area and adjacent counties. Widespread wind damage to trees and utility lines was noted, particularly across Owen County where an estimated gust of 55 knots (63 mph) downed a significant number of trees and powerlines. Further north, an estimated 60 mph gust in Boone County was followed by a measured gust of 53 knots (61 mph) at the Indianapolis Executive Airport north of Zionsville at 1335 EST.  Power lines were also downed in Hamilton County before the primary severe wind threat subsided.||In addition to the damaging winds, torrential downpours dropped widespread 2.00 to 3.00 inches of rain across the region, producing significant areal and flash flooding from mid-afternoon into the evening.  Knox County was impacted first, where roughly 2.00 inches of rainfall caused water to flow over State Roads 58 and 67, flooded local intersections from Bruceville to Oaktown, and caused manholes to overflow. As the heavy rainfall progressed eastward, county-wide road flooding developed across Putnam, Hancock, Marion, and Owen Counties, with the latter reporting up to 3.00 inches.  The most severe hydrological impact occurred in Morgan County, where approximately 3.00 inches of rainfall inundated a residential home, requiring the deployment of sandbags to combat the rising floodwaters.
episodes.212058: Supercell thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and near a warm front during the afternoon and evening hours of May 18.  The storms produced 7 documented tornadoes and eventually evolved into a line of storms that produced damaging winds of 60-80 mph across northeast and east central Kansas.  Some areas also received 2-5 inches of rain just two to three hours causing flash flooding in several areas including the city of Manhattan.
episodes.212083: A lee trough ignited widely scattered thunderstorms that produced locally damaging wind gusts over western Maryland, eastern West Virginia, and northwestern Virginia.
episodes.212086: A lee trough ignited widely scattered thunderstorms that produced locally damaging wind gusts over western Maryland, eastern West Virginia, and northwestern Virginia.
episodes.212087: A lee trough ignited widely scattered thunderstorms that produced locally damaging wind gusts over western Maryland, eastern West Virginia, and northwestern Virginia.
episodes.212297: A squall line moved through the Great Lakes region, sparking showers and thunderstorms.
episodes.212352: A line of storms developed along a cold front Sunday afternoon, stretching from South Dakota all the way down through central Kansas. As the storms progressed eastward through the evening, they moved into a favorable environment for tornado and severe wind development. Several tornadoes were observed across northeast Iowa, southeast South Dakota, and extreme southern Minnesota. There were two tornadoes in Freeborn County and one tornado in Martin County.||In addition to the tornadoes, there were reports of wind damage across southern MN. Minor structural damage and scattered tree damage suggest wind speeds around 60 to 75 mph were likely tied to the thunderstorms.
episodes.212402: An approaching mid-level disturbance broke a weak cap and allowed storms to erupt during the afternoon along a slow moving frontal boundary. These storms rapidly organized into short bowing segments and then became highly linear across northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota during the evening. Initial supercell storms produced large hail with as much as 2000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, but DCAPE of around 750-1000 J/kg allowed for the development of organized cold pools and an increasing wind threat. Several brief and highly visible tornadic spin-ups developed along the line of storms by late afternoon and evening across far eastern South Dakota, northwest Iowa and southwest Minnesota.||In addition, repeated thunderstorms brought as much as 2-4 inches of rain in a short period of time to portions of Plymouth and southern Sioux County in northwest Iowa. This same area had also received locally heavy rainfall during the previous days, resulting in spotty flooding of already saturated locations.
episodes.212652: Thunderstorms trained over portions of Barton, Russell, Ellsworth, and Lincoln counties during the afternoon and evening hours of May 17th. Several reports of large hail and flash flooding were received. The largest hail report was near Milberger in Russell County with a size of 2.25 inches in diameter.
episodes.212799: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the late morning of May 18th producing severe wind gusts, wind damage and one brief tornado.
episodes.212800: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across northwest Indiana during the late morning and early afternoon of May 18th producing scattered severe wind gusts and isolated large hail.
episodes.212801: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across southern Lake Michigan during the late morning and early afternoon of May 18th.
episodes.213122: A thunderstorm complex moved south into eastern Missouri during the early morning of May 18th. Isolated wind damage occurred as wind gusts up to 71 kts blew through the area. Rain lasted the rest of the day, resulting in minor flooding in Warren county.
episodes.213123: A thunderstorm complex moved south through Illinois during the day of May 18th. Isolated wind damage occurred in Montgomery County, and isolated flooding occurred in Marion County.
episodes.213146: A line of severe thunderstorms exited Illinois and tracked through Indiana and southern Michigan. Wind gusts near 60 mph were reported, downing trees and powerlines.
episodes.213147: A line of severe thunderstorms exited Illinois and tracked through Indiana and southern Michigan. Wind gusts near 60 mph were reported.
episodes.213149: A line of severe thunderstorms exited Illinois and tracked through Indiana and southern Michigan. Wind gusts near 60 mph were reported, downing trees and powerlines.
episodes.213370: A few (brief) thunderstorms formed off of a dryline across portions of western Oklahoma during the evening of the 18th, producing intermittent reports of large hail and severe thunderstorm winds. Towards the initial hours of the 19th, an organized convective line moved into portions of far northern Oklahoma, producing wind damage across portions of Kay County, near Newkirk.
episodes.213379: A strong upper level trough moved into the Rockies on May 18, with southwest flow aloft over the Missouri Ozarks. A cluster of thunderstorms pushed southeast into portions of central Missouri, bringing heavy rainfall and flash flooding to St. Clair, Benton, and Camden counties. Additionally, a low level jet axis extending from the Gulf through eastern Kansas strengthened overnight into May 19 while interacting with the upper level trough and a surface front. As a result, a second line of thunderstorms formed across northern Kansas, moving into Missouri overnight before exiting the state in the late afternoon hours. With the multiple rounds of heavy rainfall, storm total rainfall observations ranged between 3-7 inches across portions of southeast Kansas and the Missouri Ozarks, with 8.20 inches of rainfall measured in Hickory County. This led to multiple road closures reported from the flooding.
episodes.213426: Several clusters of severe storms developed along a slow moving cold front as it creeped across the area through the afternoon and into the nighttime hours. These storms produced up to 2-inch hail along with estimated winds up to 90 mph. Multiple structures were damaged across south-central Kansas due to these storms.
episodes.213442: During the early evening hours on the 17th, an isolated severe thunderstorm moved east out of east-central Colorado and into northwest Kansas, ahead of a strong cold front approaching from the northwest. Large hail up to ping-pong ball size was reported in Sherman County.
episodes.213505: A strong storms system passing to our north resulted in a decaying mesoscale convective system moving across the area late in the night from May 17 into the 18th. Part of the this system re-intensified over eastern Iowa producing isolated damaging wind gusts and large hail up to the size of a half dollar.
episodes.213515: Severe thunderstorms produced damaging wind gusts across southwest Iowa on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Although mid-level winds were somewhat weak���resulting in unimpressive 0���6 km bulk shear���low-level hodographs featured ample cyclonic curvature. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. As the severe squall line pushed across the Missouri River into western Iowa during the mid-to-late evening hours of May 17, it maintained its intensity and continued to produce damaging straight-line winds. Personal weather stations across the region captured a series of severe gusts as the system swept eastward. Early in the evening, a 62 mph gust was measured near Rodney in Monona County, followed shortly by a 65 mph gust near Missouri Valley in Harrison County. As the storms progressed further southeast, the winds remained severe, with a 60 mph gust recorded near Oakland in Pottawattamie County and a localized peak gust of 72 mph measured southeast of Henderson in Montgomery County before the complex eventually exited the area.
episodes.213516: Severe thunderstorms produced hail, damaging wind gusts, and tornadoes across eastern Nebraska on May 17, 2026. On this day, an upper-level trough axis remained well to the west, but an embedded shortwave and attendant jet streak ejected from eastern Colorado into eastern Nebraska. At the surface, an elongated trough extended from a low in southeast Colorado through south-central Nebraska into southeast South Dakota, acting as a persistent focus for strong deep moist convergence. During the afternoon, a narrow dryline surged into central Nebraska and Kansas. East of the boundary, warm-sector dewpoints recovered into the mid-to-upper 60s, yielding a highly unstable environment with 3,000 to 4,000 J/kg of MLCAPE. Although mid-level winds were somewhat weak���resulting in unimpressive 0���6 km bulk shear���low-level hodographs featured ample cyclonic curvature. This provided sufficient low-level shear to keep updrafts organized and separated from downdrafts despite the weaker flow aloft.||A broken line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed across east-central Nebraska during the afternoon, pushing eastwards and growing upscale into a formidable wind-producing convective system. The storms initially presented a mixed hazard of large hail and damaging winds as they impacted counties including Madison, Platte, Cuming, and Saline. Hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) was reported near Wisner, while quarter-size hail fell in several surrounding communities. Three EF-1 tornadoes were also confirmed across eastern Nebraska in Thurston, Saunders and Cass county. However, severe straight-line winds quickly became the dominant threat. Wind gusts consistently measured between 60 and 70 mph caused widespread tree damage, snapping large branches with noticeable tree damage reported in communities like Friend, Crete, and Fairbury.||As the line surged eastward through the mid-to-late evening, the severe wind threat pushed straight through the Lincoln and Omaha metropolitan areas before crossing the Missouri River into western Iowa. An automated station at the Lincoln Airport measured a 68 mph wind gust, while emergency managers and spotters reported 70 mph gusts across Lancaster and Sarpy counties. These intense winds resulted in minor structural damage, including a torn gutter on a home in Lincoln and a damaged street light in La Vista. The Omaha Eppley Airfield recorded a 63 mph gust as the storms swept through the metro. By late evening, the system accelerated across southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, producing severe wind gusts of 71 mph in Pawnee County, Nebraska, before finally weakening and exiting the region.
episodes.213580: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across Lower Michigan during the afternoon hours on Monday, May 18th.  These storms brought strong and damaging winds, which resulted in numerous areas sustaining straight-line wind damage.  Damage included numerous trees and large tree limbs downed, as well as powerlines.
episodes.213590: Easterly sea breeze convection produces a strong marine gust over Tampa Bay.
episodes.213663: A strong high pressure system centered to the south of Fiji moved a trough from the south of American Samoa onto the territorial islands on May 16th through the 18th. This stationary weather pattern lead to over 9.68 inches of rain recorded at WFO American Samoa. This includes 3.55 inches that fell in two hours on the afternoon of the 18th. This intense rainfall led to widespread flash flooding throughout the territory. Multiple landslides were also reported due to the intense rainfall on saturated soils.
episodes.213743: Thunderstorms moving through Saginaw Bay and southern Lake Huron produced wind gusts around 50 knots.
episodes.213745: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced damaging winds gusts and hail across southwest Iowa. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska, eventually pushing into southwest Iowa by 4:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster.||The primary hazards with this portion of the severe complex were large hail and significant straight-line winds. Residents in communities such as Farragut and College Springs reported hail up to ping-pong ball size (1.50 inches). Meanwhile, the bowing segments of the storm complex continued to produce extreme downdrafts, highlighted by an 84 mph wind gust measured by a personal weather station northeast of Shambaugh. The storms tracked eastward into the evening hours.
episodes.213746: On the afternoon of May 18, severe thunderstorms produced tornadoes, damaging winds gusts, hail and flash flooding across southeast Nebraska. a strong shortwave trough ejected eastward across the region, providing robust forcing for large-scale ascent. Despite lingering morning cloud cover, very steep mid-level lapse rates combined with the daytime heating of a moist low-level airmass to generate strong instability south of an advancing cold front. Mesoanalysis revealed strong theta-e advection extending from central Kansas through southeast Nebraska and southwest Iowa, highlighting the rapid return of a highly volatile environment. Thunderstorms initially initiated on the warm side of the boundary over northwest Kansas before additional development began over far southeast Nebraska by 2:00 PM CST. This convection initially exhibited discrete supercell characteristics before eventually transitioning into a broader multicell cluster. Additional cells developed north of the cold front across eastern Nebraska, bringing primarily an isolated hail threat. ||The system dropped large hail up to golf ball size (1.75 inches) and generated destructive straight-line winds, including a measured peak gust of 90 mph. The initial supercell storm mode was particularly prolific for tornadogenesis, resulting in 8 tornado across southeast Nebraska. While several of these tornadoes were brief, others caused concentrated damage to trees, farm outbuildings, and irrigation pivots���most notably in Johnson, Nemaha, and Richardson counties. In several instances, these tornadoes were embedded within even broader swaths of intense 80 to 95 mph downburst winds. As the storms transitioned into a messy multicell cluster, torrential downpours also triggered isolated reports of flash flooding.
episodes.213748: Thunderstorms moving through Lake St. Clair produced wind gusts in excess of 40 knots.
episodes.213750: A thunderstorm moving through western Lake Erie produced a wind gusts around 45 knots.

episodes.213776: During the evening on May 17th severe storms moved out of northern Iowa and into southeast Minnesota. As they moved into Mower County, winds gusts to around 60 mph were observed in the Austin area. Additional tree damage was noted in the Lewiston area as these storms moved through.
episodes.213968: As the third week of May 2026 unfolded, the dynamic breakup front stalled repeatedly along the Lower Yukon, creating a cascading sequence of severe jams and flooding. This period involved massive downstream surges as well as backwater effects in tributaries like the Andreafsky and Chuilnuk.
episodes.213993: An outflow boundary interacting with a seasonably warm and moist airmass triggered a line of strong to severe thunderstorms across western Illinois during the morning of May 18th.  The storms pushed eastward across central Illinois, resulting in periodic damaging wind gusts mainly north of the I-70 corridor.  While the leading edge of the storms swept eastward into Indiana, the trailing flank became parallel with the prevailing flow and led to training cells and heavy rainfall along and south of I-70.  Widespread amounts of 2 to 4 inches were common, with portions of southern Effingham County and northern Clay County picking up in excess of 5 inches.  An observer 3 miles north-northwest of Bible Grove in far southern Effingham County measured 5.50.  As a result of the excessive rainfall over the course of just a couple hours, flash flooding occurred across this area.
episodes.214091: A line of thunderstorms swept across Lake Erie during the afternoon and evening of Monday, May 18, 2026. Several severe thunderstorms within this line generated marine wind gusts over Lake Erie.
episodes.214107: A line of thunderstorms swept across Lake Erie during the afternoon and evening of Monday, May 18, 2026. Several severe thunderstorms within this line generated thunderstorm wind damage and wind gusts across Northern Ohio.
episodes.214137: On May 18th into May 19th, the Ohio Valley was in the middle of a southwest mid- and upper-level flow regime between troughing over the central CONUS and southeast US ridging. Smaller scale perturbations within the broader flow pattern would support a couple waves of showers and thunderstorms, with isolated strong to severe storms occurring across north central Kentucky and southern Indiana during the afternoon and evening hours both days. On May 18th, storms which initially developed as scattered cells over southern Illinois merged into a line across southern Indiana. This line of storms had a modest amount of instability and vertical wind shear to support it, with temperatures in the upper 80s and dewpoint temperatures in the upper 60s supporting 1500-2000 J/kg of mixed-layer CAPE. Scattered wind damage was observed across southern Indiana, with the greatest concentration of damage occurring in Dubois and Washington County, where several trees were blown down. Additional rounds of showers and thunderstorms later in the evening would also lead to a few occurrences of flash flooding, especially along tributaries of the Blue River in Washington County.
episodes.214247: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms moved across Lower Michigan on Monday, May 18th.  These storms brought strong and damaging winds, which resulted in wind damage and a large number of power outages.
episodes.214335: A thunderstorm produced a strong wind gust along the St Lucie County coast.
episodes.214391: During the afternoon hours of May 17th, storms brought damaging wind gusts to portions of NW Missouri.
episodes.214398: A slow moving frontal boundary from northeast Nebraska into northwest Iowa focused development of scattered thunderstorms during the late afternoon and very early evening.  Storms fired and intensified with elevated instability above a stratus layer around 1000-1500 J/kg and 40-50 knots of effective shear.  Stronger and more organized cells produced large hail up to golf ball size.
episodes.214399: A slow moving frontal boundary from northeast Nebraska into northwest Iowa focused development of scattered thunderstorms during the late afternoon and very early evening. Stronger and more organized cells produced large hail up to golf ball size.
episodes.214400: A slow moving frontal boundary from northeast Nebraska into northwest Iowa focused development of scattered thunderstorms during the late afternoon and very early evening. Storms fired and intensified with elevated instability above a stratus layer around 1000-1500 J/kg and 40-50 knots of effective shear. Stronger and more organized cells produced large hail up to golf ball size. Back on the cooler side of the boundary, only smaller hail occurred.

A tornado developed in open fields near the intersection of 625 Avenue and 725 Road, and moved quickly east. The tornado damaged many trees, flipped pivots, and destroyed at least two large farm sheds. The damage along the track was somewhat sporadic at times, and this concentrated area of tornado damage was embedded within a much broader area of 60 to 80 mph winds in the downdraft regions of the parent thunderstorm. The peak width of the tornado was determined where it traveled through a long line of trees and gave evidence to the most intense focused zone of winds being approximately 200 yards wide. Maximum wind speeds were estimated at 97 mph. The tornado continued into Nemaha county before dissipating at 3:11 PM CST.

In the late afternoon and early evening of May 18, 2026, severe thunderstorms and heavy rain triggered flash flooding across central Gage County. Because the area was already saturated from several consecutive days of rain, the ground could not absorb the sudden deluge. Driven by intense downpours of 1 to 2 inches per hour, total accumulations rapidly reached 3.00 to 4.50 inches.
